Cassandra. The princess of Troy blessed with prophecy but cursed that no one would believe her, making her the archetype of the unheeded prophet.

Cassandra was the daughter of Priam and Hecuba, and she was blessed with the gift of prophecy. But the god Apollo cursed her after she rejected his romantic advances. His curse transformed her gift into a terrible burden: no one would ever believe what she said, no matter how accurate her visions proved to be.

When the Greeks brought the wooden horse to the gates of Troy, Cassandra warned the Trojans against bringing it into the city, knowing it contained enemy soldiers. But the people dismissed her warnings, and the horse was taken inside. Troy burned exactly as she had predicted, and her words were proven accurate only in destruction. After the war, Cassandra was enslaved to Agamemnon and taken to Mycenae as his concubine. Upon arrival in Greece, she was murdered, either by Agamemnon's wife Clytemnestra or alongside him.

Cassandra's tragedy lies in being right at the wrong time. A prophet whose wisdom saved no one, she remains eternally connected to those who shaped her suffering. Priam, her father, was the king who refused to heed her warnings. Hecuba, her mother, was a fellow victim of prophetic knowledge and powerlessness. Hector, her brother, was someone whose death she foresaw. Paris, another brother, was the one who abducted Helen, an action she warned would doom Troy. Agamemnon, the Greek leader, enslaved and ultimately murdered her. And Apollo, the god who cursed her, transformed her gift into torment.
